newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ruling party rolls to massive poll win.
newsitem.headline: Singapore ruling party rolls to massive poll win.

text.p: Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong's ruling party smashed aside opposition challenges in Singapore's general election, allowing just two seats to escape its grasp.
The final result early on Friday showed a close win for his People's Action Party juggernaut in a multi-member constituency where he had rolled out his heaviest weapons.

Goh, who had laid his prestige on the line to keep the opposition presence in parliament to a minimum and conducted a ferocious campaign focused on voters' pockets and sensitive racial issues, was jubilant.
"This is a watershed election," he told a news conference. Voters, he said, "have rejected Western-style liberal democracy and freedoms, putting individual rights over that of society."
The PAP won the election before a vote was cast when opposition parties decided to contest only 36 of parliament's 83 seats. They had held four seats in the old assembly.
But Goh said at the start of the nine-day election campaign he did not want opposition members in parliament disrupting the progress of a country the PAP has made into a prosperous, modern nation.

He swept aside opposition attempts to focus voters' minds on such things as a rising cost of living and the need for curbs on the PAP, which has ruled Singapore since it became self-governing in 1959.

His opening blast was a stern warning to voters that failure to support the PAP would mean losing out on a multi-billion dollar programme to renovate housing estates that would increase the value of their homes.
That brought criticism from the U.S. State Department, which a furious Goh accused of interfering.

Then Goh unleashed the PAP's considerable force on the constituency of Cheng San, where five seats were at stake in a winner-takes-all contest and the left-leaning Workers' Party was seen as having its best hope.

He accused one Workers' Party candidate, Tang Liang Hong, of being a "Chinese chauvinist" who was a danger to the harmony of multi-racial Singapore, which is 77 percent ethnic Chinese with significant Malay and Tamil minorities.
Tang, he alleged, had said the ethnic Chinese were "carrying the sedan chair" instead of sitting on it.

That, he charged, was an attempt to "divide society along ethnic and linguistic lines" that had to be nipped in the bud because with the rising influence of China and its language, the temptation to make the tongue dominant in Singapore would grow.
"As the majority, Chinese must always be sensitive to the minorities. We are not a Chinese country and we must never allow Chinese chauvinism to turn us into one," he said.
There were other successes for Goh, who had said defeat in Cheng San would diminish his credibility at home and abroad.
He had also made a determined effort to keep Singapore Democratic Party leader Chee Soon Juan out of parliament, calling him a "proven liar".
Chee won only a third of the vote in the single-member constituency where he stood.

Political analysts had also said that in the absence of any suspense over the election winner, a key point of interest would be whether the PAP share of the vote would continue its slow decline from 75 percent in 1980 to 61 percent in 1991.
This time, it rose to 65 percent.
